newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coffee roasters caught in margin squeeze.
newsitem.headline: German coffee roasters caught in margin squeeze.

text.p: German coffee roasters fear that rising green coffee prices will ruin their profit margins as retail prices of roasted coffee are still falling, traders said on Monday.
"Futures and differentials are rising but there is no money to be made in coffee...something will have to be done," one trader said.
"The situation calls for retail price increases but no one dares to make the first move in this competitive environment... perhaps price increases will have to wait until the second quarter."
Roasters were also hard hit by dollar gains, which lifted mark-denominated buying prices.
Average retail prices of roasted coffee have fallen from 6.80 marks per 0.5 kg to below 6.00 marks in some cases.
Retail prices dropped by 10 percent last year while roasters' buying-in prices rose by an estimated 15 percent, according to industry figures.
Fund and roaster buying boosted arabica futures last week and a Colombian strike also supported prices.
New York March settled at 124.00 cents a lb, up 0.95 on the day last Friday.
Traders believed the market was set for further rises, possibly after a short-term correction which could lose it 10 cents.
Robustas, which are less important in German blends, also looked set to make further futures gains.
Some consumers fear an emergency meeting of ACPC members in Brazil on January 23 may bring further export retention in the first half of 1997.
But traders here said other Latin American producers in search of coffee earnings might want to take advantage of Colombia's situation to secure themselves more market share.
Outright prices in local import markets were high, reflecting nearby tightness and a reluctance at origin to release enough material for the second half of the year.
Arabicas were up $5-7 per 50 kg fob -- with Brazils at $138 ex-origin and $134 ex-second hand -- and Vietnam robustas up $2 at $54 cif.
